why: The prompt is a Squid Game clone built as a sequence of discrete elimination rounds ('Game 1: Motion Sensor Rush', 'Game 2: Gravity Fractures') with 30 bots, which is the round-based minigame pattern party-casual describes; 'action' misses that nothing here is combat.

Every mechanic named is traversal - Dash, Slide, Grapple, Sandevistan time-slow - and the map spec asks for ledges, rooftops and neon pipes 'perfectly spaced out so the player can seamlessly chain' them. There is no enemy or weapon in the prompt, so obby-platformer beats action.
'A destruction game with a big city to destroy' names no opponent, weapon or objective, just a sandbox to wreck, which is the destruction-simulator pattern rather than action combat.

The prompt says 'third-person co-op roguelite shooter' and specifies crosshair aiming, an automatic assault rifle, magazines, reserve ammo and damage falloff. The spreadsheet's own vocabulary has a shooter category and it did not use it here.

A tornado tearing through a city where you shelter in houses and use interceptor vehicles is the storm-survival loop; the hazard is weather, not an enemy to fight, so 'action' fits worse than survival.

Despite the words 'role playing experience', the stated activities are tending gardens, trading vegetables and owning a hobbit burrow with friends - cozy life sim with no combat, quests or levels, which is roleplay-avatar-sim rather than rpg.

Explicit hydration and hunger bars that you refill from lakes and rivers, plus hunting hares and squirrels, is the survival meter loop; nothing in the prompt has quests, levels or character progression to justify rpg.

The request is 100 dragons, many islands and the alpha dragons - creature collection and island exploration - with no combat, classes, questing or leveling named, so adventure fits the prompt as written better than rpg.

The prompt self-declares 'Open-world Action RPG / Survival' and lists quests, leveling, bosses, loot, crafting, unlockable abilities and dungeon raids. Our 'simulation' label (and the plot-isolated shape) misreads a full RPG spec.

Blox Fruits is a leveling combat RPG with stats, quests and boss grinding, and its First Sea is that game's low-level questing region; adventure understates the progression systems the reference implies.

The loop is mining ores in progressively deeper cave zones with a glowing pickaxe, display cases and leaderboards - a mining simulator with hub-and-zone gating, not the quests, classes or combat that rpg implies.

Apocalypse Rising 2 is a zombie-apocalypse looter-survival game, and the prompt's whole ask is spawn weapons plus a big map with civilian/Soviet/military/special loot tiers to scavenge - survival looting, not rpg progression.

This is the Steal-a-Brainrot pattern: a personal base plot, pets bought from a carpet that generate value, and stealing from other players' bases. That is a collection/tycoon sim loop; nothing here is avatar roleplay.

Crystals mined from themed caves hatch pets whose 'unique abilities' feed back into mining faster and jumping higher, with trading and rarest-collected leaderboards - a pet/mining simulator economy rather than avatar roleplay.

Buying dog breeds from a shop by rarity tier ('the rarest is a greyhound') and spawning them into your own pen is a collection sim; the player is a collector managing stock, not roleplaying as or with an avatar pet.
The prompt literally asks for a 'pet simulator' with egg hatching from the ground, zone prices, auto-hatch and huge pets - the canonical Pet Simulator upgrade loop.
Opening eggs and breaking lucky blocks for money to buy more pets, with 12 zones gated behind pet count, is a pure simulator progression ladder rather than avatar roleplay.

Playing vet with a check-in desk, medicine and hospital floors is a job-roleplay setup, but the lobby pads capped at 5 players read as a matchmade job-sim round; the prompt is too thin - no avatar customization, no patient roles - to separate the two.

Despite the word 'simulator' in the title, the described skill is precise aerodynamic control leaping from massive towers to avoid impact failure, which is tower geometry and movement precision; there is no economy or upgrade loop to make it a simulation.

The prompt says in capitals that ONLY the lobby is being built - a retro-styled hub with a matchmaking portal, spawn zone and room-creation GUI. Labeling the deliverable 'shooter' describes a game that this request explicitly defers.
Three words - 'make a zombie arena' - name no weapon, so guns (shooter) and simply outlasting the horde (survival) are equally supportable readings.

The player is locked to one axis with two lanes of enemies and upgrade walls approaching, which is the lane-runner form, but the only verb in the prompt is shooting and you die by failing to kill what is in front of you; both labels catch half of it.

You steer a rolling tyre with left and right only, down a winding mountain path, against the clock, restarting if you leave the path - vehicle handling on a descent route. There is no jumping or platform placement, which is what obby_and_platformer would require.

There is a measured track with laps and a furthest-studs board (racing-shaped), but no opponent, and the real driver is pets and treadmills buying a speed multiplier; the spreadsheet's obby_and_platformer catches the sliding traversal while ours catches the track, and neither names the upgrade loop.

Collecting brainrots, carrying them to a safe zone while bigger ones chase you, and placing them on a base to generate money is the Steal-a-Brainrot collection economy; there is no course or platforming in the prompt.

The prompt is a keyboard-map speed game: press buttons for money, buy speed, then get past the obstacles. The upgrade economy supports simulation and the obstacle traversal supports obby_and_platformer - this hybrid genre is genuinely both, and the prompt gives no reason to prefer either half.

Each round you earn a budget and place hazards - blades, boulders, wrecking balls - along a route that waves of NPCs then try to walk to the exit. That is the tower-defense loop, which is strategy; 'simulation' misses that the player is defending a lane, not running an economy.

The prompt says 'simulador de urso' and asks for run/jump/hit controls on a bear model in an open forest with day-night cycle - Roblox's simulation category and our roleplay-avatar-sim both cover animal-avatar wilderness games, so this is largely a vocabulary split.

The payoff the prompt names is joining a basketball world cup and winning against other people, which needs a court to play on; the RNG rolling is how you assemble the roster, and the spreadsheet has sports_and_racing available but did not use it.

The prompt calls itself a 'simulator' and stacks rebirths, egg-hatched pets, gamepasses and +1 speed per second, but all the described space is a jumping ascent across lava rocks, broken bridges and floating magma islands with checkpoints - the two labels each describe one real half.

'A world that people can build their dream home' is the shared-neighborhood house-building pattern, which Roblox's own taxonomy files under roleplay and avatar sim; nothing in the eight words points at a production or upgrade economy.

The user pins the format themselves - 'like steal a brainrot layout' - meaning a personal plot where hatched dinosaurs are placed and generate value, which is a collection sim rather than adventure exploration.
'A 3d garden game where you collect berries' is a gather-and-grow loop with no exploration, journey or threat, so simulation fits and adventure does not.

The core ask is making the whole town work for you to produce a key, with upgrades and rebirth - an idle production loop with prestige. The notebook-escape framing is set dressing over what is mechanically a simulator.

The prompt self-labels 'horror adventure' and lists 100+ rooms, keys, quests, shop, cutscenes and multiple endings (adventure), while the moment-to-moment loop is evading three hunting monsters using hiding spots and traps (survival); both labels describe real halves of this spec.

Murder mystery is a round game about avoiding an active killer inside a confined mansion, which survival captures; adventure implies exploration or a journey that the four-word prompt gives no sign of.

'Make the map like a story game lobby' asks only for a lobby, so no gameplay is specified at all - the spreadsheet is labeling the genre story games belong to and we are labeling the waiting-room space, and neither is testable against the prompt.

The user ends with 'it is a story game' and describes a fixed narrative with a scripted ending and a sequel tease (adventure), but the playable beats are being chased by the teacher, hunting for something to unlock the doors, and escaping the school (survival).

The prompt only names 'a high-quality map inspired by Slap Tower' plus admin-triggered events - rising lava, low gravity, fog, wind. Slap Tower's knock-players-off PvP supports action while the tower itself and the hazard events support obby_and_platformer, and no combat detail is given either way.

The tower has guns and zombies attacking you and you must defeat all the bosses before the key appears - progress is gated on combat, not on platforming skill, so action fits better than obby_and_platformer.

The user names the game a '1+ speed clicker' and the progression is upgrading anime characters with wins; the parkour course is the earning minigame inside a clicker/upgrade simulator, so simulation is the better dominant label.

Placing a crosshair, choosing bomb size and blasting an indestructible crate onto a painted target to 'pass the level' is a physics puzzle with a discrete solution per level; nothing is being fought, so action misses it.

The whole task is a vehicle speed-and-position problem along a rail route - reverse to catch up, hook up, floor it the other way - against a 10-minute timer with a derailment fail state, which is a timed route challenge rather than a train-operation sim.

The user calls it 'a word game': a word is spoken, you spell it, and you are told right or wrong - a word puzzle. The beach setting and chairs are scenery, not the party-minigame structure our label implies.
